Using the Annual Integrated Survey to recalibrate the monthly dataPosted on November 5, 2026

SHARE THIS PAGE:

Link Copied

The takeaway
Data agencies often recalibrate speedier, high-frequency survey data with lower-frequency, more-comprehensive efforts. The Census does this with its Annual Integrated Economic Survey.
The data
Our FRED graph above compares two sets of Census survey data: their Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES) retail trade sales data (blue line) and their Monthly Retail Trade Survey data (green line). If you add up the 12 monthly values for any year, you get the AIES annual total for that year, within a few million dollars. That's not a big difference if you consider the annual values are in the trillions. In 2024, the latest full-year data available at the time of this writing, both came to about $7.107 trillion.
How does the annual survey sharpen the monthly survey data?
The AIES works as a foundational benchmark. Monthly and quarterly Census surveys are built for speed: They use smaller samples and are best at measuring change from one period to the next. After the monthly surveys are taken, the AIES uses a much larger sample and more detail and recalibrates the levels for those monthly surveys. That is, when new annual results arrive, the faster series are revised to match it. The AIES also updates the Census Business Register, the master list from which other economic surveys draw their samples.
Other statistical agencies perform similar adjustments. The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses this process to derive industry output for gross domestic product (GDP) data. The Bureau of Labor Statistics uses it for the producer price index and productivity measures. And the Federal Reserve Board uses it for their index of industrial production.
The scope of the AIES
FRED recently added 5,582 series from the AIES. Starting in 2023, the AIES replaced seven separate annual business surveys with one, which is sent to approximately 359,000 companies. The data in FRED cover revenues, expenses, payroll, and employment for 1,046 economic activities across seven industries: agriculture, construction, manufacturing, mining, retail, services, and wholesale trade. Many series go back well before 2023, because the Census folded in results from the legacy surveys: retail and wholesale to 1992, manufacturing to 2007, and services to 2013.
More details about the AIES can be found on the Census website.
How this graph was created: Search FRED for and select “Retail Trade: Sales.” Click the “Edit Graph” button and select the “Add Line” tab to search for “Retail Sales: Retail Trade.” Don’t forget to click “Add data series.”
